The XPS spectrum of the sample before TiO2 deposition. The carbon and oxygen signals located at 285 eV and 530 eV may come from the adsorbed contaminants on the surface. There appears a weak peak at 397 eV, which is the characteristic 1 s photoelectron line of nitrogen. It is noteworthy that besides Cr, there appear signals from Fe and Mn in the spectrum. Since no such impurities are intentionally introduced into the CrN film, we think that Fe and Mn come from the stainless steel substrate. It is widely accepted that XPS measurements can only detect the signals from the top-surface of samples in the depth of tens of angstroms. Therefore it is thought that the CrN coating may have some through-thickness cracks or pinholes. For the TiO2/CrN double-layer coated sample, the XPS spectrum of which is shown in Fig. 2b. Signals from Fe, Cr and Mn are invisible in the spectrum. Just as that in Fig. 2 a, the carbon may come from the surface contaminants. The absence of the signals from Cr, Mn, and Fe indicates that the TiO2 layer shields the layer underneath entirely, and the through-thickness cracks or pinholes in the CrN layer have been blocked. The XRD patterns of the CrN/S.S before and after the TiO2 deposition are shown in Fig. 3a. The peaks at 44.1 and 51.4° in both spectra come from the (111) and (200) facet of the cubic phased stainless steel (JCPDS: 33 –0397). The pattern for the CrN single-layer coated stainless steel shows only peaks from the stainless steels, which indicates that the CrN layer may be amorphous. While for the TiO2/CrN coated sample, besides the peaks from the substrate, there appear a series of peaks located at 25.35°, 38.70°, 48.10° and 55.20°. All these peaks can be indexed to anatase TiO2 (JCPDS: 84–1285), indicating that the TiO2 film is crystallized in anatase structure. To confirm the structure of the TiO2 layer, Raman measurements are conducted on the TiO2/CrN/S.S under back-scattering configuration at room temperature, as shown in Fig. 3b. All the five peaks can be attributed to the vibration mode of anatase TiO2, confirming that the TiO2 deposition is crystallized in anatase structure. The polarization curves of potential (relative to SCE) versus current density of the CrN coated stainless steel samples before and after the TiO2 deposition in 3.0 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution, the plot of bare stainless steel is also presented as a reference. The equilibrium corrosion potential (Ecorr) is −0.95 V, and the corrosion current density is 2.6 × 10−6 mA/cm2 for the bare stainless steel. For the CrN single-layer coated stainless steel, Ecorr is about −0.74 V, while for the double-layer coated sample, it is −0.49 V. The positive shift of Ecorr reveals the increase in corrosion resistance. Corrosion current density is an important parameter to assess the kinetics of corrosion reaction, and it is normally proportional to the corrosion rate. It can be seen from the polarization curves that in most cases, the current density of the double-layer coated sample is smaller than that of the single-layer coated one. The corrosion current density decreases from 1.9 × 10−6 mA/cm2 for CrN/S.S to 3.1 × 10−7 mA/cm2 for TiO2/CrN/S.S, which implies that the existence of the conformal TiO2 deposition can help to decrease the corroding rate of the stainless steel. We think the improvement in corrosion resistance may due to the fact that the TiO2 layer blocks the through-thickness cracks or pinholes in the CrN layer, which will prevent the direct attacking of the corrosive media, thus retard the corroding of the stainless steel.

Alumina was deposited by ALD in a Beneq TFS-500 reactor using 10 to 1000 growth cycles of either trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water, or TMA and ozone. The deposition temperature was 220 °C and pressure approximately 5 mbar (500 Pa).

The dielectric layer is either aluminum oxide deposited by ALD, or silicon dioxide deposited by PECVD. Both are low-temperature processes compatible with metals and glass substrates.

HECL measurements were made in a round sample cell of 5.6 mm diameter. Electrical contact to the working electrode was made from the wafer backside for silicon samples, or directly to the metal thin film for samples on a glass substrate. The electrode was pulsed using a custom made coulostatic pulse generator at a rate of 20 Hz, as detailed in.

The main outlier is tungsten, which exhibits a positive thickness offset in ALD and a relatively small negative offset in PECVD, and should therefore be expected to perform better as a tunnel dielectric. However, as the higher observed deposition rate over tungsten suggests, the metal is likely being oxidized at the metal/dielectric interface.

The difference in optimal film thickness for HECL between alumina dielectrics produced by TMA/H2O and TMA/O3 ALD processes is notable. The optimal dielectric thickness over a silicon electrode is drastically lower for the ozone process, and a significant difference is also seen over aluminum (Figs. 1 and 2).

We investigate the effects of adding hydrogen to tungsten hexafluoride (WF6) during atomic layer deposition (ALD) on silicon dioxide (SiO2) and silicon (Si) substrates. The addition of H2 impairs nucleation on SiO2, while having no effect on growth on Si. We demonstrate that the gas-phase production of hydrogen fluoride (HF) is responsible for this phenomenon. By analyzing the effects of ALD reaction chemistry on film nucleation, we expand the selectivity window by at least 10 cycles and enable an additional 6 nm of selective tungsten deposition on desired surfaces.

This article presents a study on the initial growth mechanism of nickel sulfide (NiS) on silicon oxide (SiOx) using atomic layer deposition (ALD). The authors investigate the surface chemistry and morphology of the NiS films deposited at different stages of ALD. They propose a reaction-agglomeration scheme to explain the initial growth behavior, which involves the conversion of nickel-oxide (NiOx) to nickel-sulfide (NiS) in the presence of hydrogen sulfide (H2S). The authors also use LEIS and TEM to confirm the proposed mechanism. The study provides valuable insights into the surface chemistry and morphology of NiS films deposited by ALD, which is essential for understanding the performance of NiS-based devices.

The initial atomic layer deposition (ALD) growth of nickel sulfide (NiS) on silicon oxide (SiOx) was investigated. The ALD process employed bis(N,N'-di-tert-butylacetamidinato)nickel(II) (Ni(amd)2)) and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) as precursors at a deposition temperature of 200°C. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and low-energy ion scattering (LEIS) were used to characterize the surface chemistry of the NiS films deposited by varying numbers of ALD cycles. This article presents the results of a study on the atomic layer deposition (ALD) of aluminum phosphate thin films. The authors used a 200 mm ALD reactor and a commercial dimethylaluminum isopropoxide precursor to deposit AlPO4 thin films on silicon substrates. The films were characterized using various techniques, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The results show that the ALD process produces high-quality AlPO4 thin films with a stoichiometry of 2:1 Al:PO4. The authors also investigated the effects of substrate temperature, precursor flow rate, and plasma exposure time on the film properties. The study demonstrates the potential of ALD for the deposition of high-quality aluminum phosphate thin films.

We report the growth of Zn(O,S) thin films using atomic layer deposition (ALD) techniques to produce tunable band gaps. Alternating cycles of ZnO ALD and ZnS ALD were initially used to deposit the Zn(O,S) films. The composition of the Zn(O,S) alloys deposited using the alternating cycle method was not easy to control. The problem is an efficient surface exchange reaction between ZnO and gaseous H2S given by: ZnOH* + H2S → ZnSH* + H2O. This exchange reaction produces much higher sulfur content in the Zn(O,S) films than expected based on the ratio of ZnO ALD and ZnS ALD cycles.

Zn(O,S) thin films were grown using atomic layer deposition (ALD) techniques to produce tunable band gaps. Alternating cycles of ZnO ALD and ZnS ALD were initially used to deposit the Zn(O,S) films. The composition of the Zn(O,S) alloys deposited using the alternating cycle method was not easy to control. The problem is an efficient surface exchange reaction between ZnO and gaseous H2S given by: ZnOH* + H2S -> ZnSH* + H2O. This exchange reaction produces much higher sulfur content in the Zn(O,S) films than expected based on the ratio of ZnO ALD and ZnS ALD cycles. An alternative method of growing the Zn(O,S) thin films was then explored that uses coZ dosing of H2O and H2S at 100°C. This coZdosing method produced different compositions of the Zn(O,S) film by varying the mole fraction of the dosing mixture. The coZdosing method controlled the Zn(O,S) alloy composition much more accurately than the alternating cycle method. The band gaps for Zn(O,S) thin films were measured using the alternating cycle or coZ dosing method. The band gaps could be produced with the most control by the mole fraction of H2S in the H2S/H2O coZdosing mixture.

We report the growth of pure, metallic gold nanoparticles using a plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD) process. The PEALD process exhibits saturation of the precursor and reactant halfcycles on gold seed layers with a steady growth rate of 0.030 pm per cycle. A similar steady growth rate is obtained on bare SiO2 surfaces, after a sufficient number of cycles. The chemistry-speci ﬁc (surface structure, precursor molecules, and reaction agent) saturated deposition rate (deposited amount per cycle) with respect to the precursor and reactionagent pulses is the key feature that characterize the atomic layer deposition (ALD).

1 However, the surface chemistry in ALD is generally very complicated involving the surface reaction sites, gas phase molecules, reaction byproducts, and the exchange of electric charges between the surface and precursor molecules.

An even more complicating factor could be the involvement of a substrate material or previously grown ﬁlm material. Di ﬀusion of a substrate material can inﬂuence the growth rate as well as the phase of the ﬁlms.

Metal oxide (MO) ﬁlms, such as NiO as in this study, are also typical materials of which ALD rate are seriously inﬂuenced by these factors, especially when the ﬁlms were grown on metal substrates of which oxides are unstable or stable against the chemical interaction with the incoming precursor molecules or growing ﬁlms.

Substrate enhanced growth of stable oxides, such as TiO and SrO, is a representative example of the involvement of a substrate into the ALD of MO ﬁlms. These ﬁlms were grown on Ru metal, which is vulnerable to oxidation during the strong oxygen source (such as O3 or plasma-enhanced O2) pulse step and is also susceptible to the reduction during the precursor pulse step.

In this case, the growth rate during initial tens of cycles was highly increased compared with the saturated steadystate growth rate, which is usually estimated from the slope of best linear ﬁtted graph of ﬁlm thickness (or mass gain) vs number of ALD cycles (ncy) when the ﬁlm becomes thick enough not to be inﬂuenced by the possible reaction with the substrate.

This was attributed to the chemical vapor deposition (CVD)-like growth of the ﬁlms during the initial cycles due to the (unwanted) supply of oxygen to the precursor molecules during the precursor pulse step, where the oxygen was supplied by the reduction of a previously oxidized Ru substrate.

5−7 This is basically due to the lower stability of the RuOx layer compared with the growing oxide ﬁlms. However, once the metal surface is completely covered with the growing ﬁlm, and the growing ﬁlms become thick enough, no more such oxygen-induced CVD-like growth is attained and the saturation growth rate is determined by the factors more inherent to ALD, such as molecule size, density of the surface adsorption site, and the reaction kinetics with oxygen, etc.

On the other hand, if the substrate material is nonreacting, such as Pt, as shown in this work, or forms highly stable oxides, such as Si, such substrate-enhanced growth is hardly observed, and even nucleation retardation is sometimes observed, which is generally an unwanted aspect of ALD.

However, there have been cases seldom reported in ALD where the saturated steady-state growth rate was still inﬂuenced by the substrate material even when the growing ﬁlms completely covered the metal surface and the ﬁlms were thick enough to suppress the oxygen exchange through the ﬁlms.

In this work, the authors studied the substrate effects on the growth rate of NiO ﬁlm via a plasma-enhanced ALD method, where the substrates are inert to the chemical reaction (Pt), interact with the growing ﬁlm only at the interface (Ru) or keep interacting with the growing ﬁlm throughout the whole growth cycles (W).

Since the NiO ﬁlms were grown simultaneously at a time by the PEALD on the three metal ﬁlms, possible process variations can hardly inﬂuence the results whereby this could be a feasible model system to examine the complicated ALD mechanism regarding MO ﬁlm depending on the types of metal electrodes.

In addition, NiO ﬁlm has been researched extensively as a resistive switching (RS) material for next generation nonvolatile memory (NVM) devices among the various binary transition metal oxides.

As reported recently, the RS phenomenon in several MO ﬁlms was triggered from the evolution of oxygen vacancy via the redox mechanism through the application of an electric field.

For the speciﬁc case of NiO, when the conducting segments create a connected network, the electrical current drastically jumped to a high level, which is usually controlled to a compliance level in order to protect the sample from complete breakdown. Therefore, this is called electroforming, which actually coincides with a controlled soft breakdown.

In contrast, the current was dropped down when the conducting network was disassembled by mostly the Joule heat eﬀect. This RS phenomenon was closely correlated with a local nonstoichiometry within the oxide ﬁlms.

Many studies, NiO ﬁlms were fabricated by reactive-sputtering or thermal oxidation of Ni metal. However, it was widely reported that the electrical properties of NiO ﬁlm are highly sensitive to the deposition parameters such as oxygen partial pressure, plasma power, and deposition temperature, which generally make the stable production of ﬂuently switching NiO ﬁlms diﬃcult.

The ALD method might be a viable solution to the reproducibility problem regarding the reactive sputtering process for NiO ﬁlm thanks to its inherent self-limiting and saturating deposition behavior. In addition, it has an advantage in adjusting the ﬁlm thickness and composition of ﬁlms with atomic level accuracy by controlling the number of deposition cycles and varying the types of oxygen source or precursor/reactant injection sequences.

Moreover, it has unprecedented step coverage over severely topological surfaces, which is a crucial factor for the development of a vertically integrated device structure as an appropriate structure for a terabit-scale NVM.

Therefore, it is necessary to study the ALD process of NiO ﬁlm in detail for manufacturing nanoscaled conformal ﬁlm as well as to improve the RS properties in ALD oxide ﬁlms for NVM application. The electrode is another crucial factor that needs to be considered for the ALD NiO ﬁlm to be used as a ﬂuent RS material.

For various reasons, RS is generally highly dependent on the types of electrode.

Ni is one of the diﬃcult metals that could have a facile ALD precursor due to its relative large atom size and heavy weight. Therefore, stable precursors having stable and simple ligand structure, such as alkyl- or alkoxy-ligands, are rare. Perhaps the most feasible Ni-precursor is cyclopentadienyl (Cp-) based ones thanks to their volatility and high reactivity.

ALD of NiO ﬁlms using Cp-based precursors were reported by several groups.

However, their research has been limited to examine the inﬂuence of deposition conditions, such as substrate temperature (Ts) and types of oxygen source on the crystal structure and composition of prepared ﬁlms. Furthermore, detailed reports on the inﬂuence of metal electrodes and the RS property of the ﬁlms are not made yet.

value: Atomic Layer Deposition of Gallium Sulphide Films for Lithium-Ion Battery Applications

Gallium sulphide films were deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) using alternating exposures to Ga2(NMe2)6 and H2SiN. The films are smooth, amorphous, and conformal on high-aspect-ratio substrates. In situ quartz crystal microbalance (QCM), quadrupole mass spectrometry (QMS), and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) measurements revealed that the growth mechanism proceeds via ligand exchange reactions, where a majority of the dimethylamido groups are released during the H2S exposures. The Ga and S are in the oxidation states expected for Ga2S3, but the S/Ga ratio is lower than expected due to residual dimethylamido ligands remaining in the film. The ALD GaSx films are relatively inert towards air exposure, and the resistance towards S/O exchange can be further improved using a 10-nm ALD Al2O3 capping layer. The resultant ALD GaSx films exhibited excellent electrochemical performance as a lithium-ion battery (LIB) anode material, showing high capacity and reliable cyclability compared to commercial Ga2S3.

value: Influence of Ge Precursor on Growth Rate and Surface Coverage in ALD of GeTe2 Layer

The influence of Ge precursor on growth rate and surface coverage in ALD of GeTe2 layer was investigated. The results show that the incorporation mechanism of the GeTe2 layer into the (GeTe2)(1-x)(Sb2Te3)x film during ALD is not a genuine ALD mechanism, but rather a physisorption process. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller-type analysis of the growth behavior reveals that the maximum physisorption density of the precursor molecules even with a multilayer configuration is still far lower than the full coverage of the monolayer, which is the fundamental reason that ALD-like saturation can be achieved even for the multilayer physisorbed Ge(OC2H5)4 molecules. The behavior of the growth rate with variations in substrate temperature and precursor bubbling temperature can also be quantitatively predicted using the physisorption model based on BET theory.

We report the fabrication and characterization of ZnO-Al2O3 and ZnO-TiO2 core-shell nanowire dyesensitized solar cells. Thin Al2O3 shells act as tunnel barriers that reduce recombination only at the expense of a larger reduction in electron injection yield and a lower device efficiency. TiO2 shells suppress recombination and markedly improve cell open-circuit voltage and fill factor. We attribute these effects to the passivation of surface recombination sites and the buildup of a radial energy barrier that repels electrons from the nanowire surface.

HCPA-ALD of AlN, GaN and AlxGa1-xNx Thin Films

This paper presents the HCPA-ALD (Hydrothermal Chemical Vapor Deposition) growth of crystalline AlN, GaN, and AlxGa1-xNx thin films at low temperatures using trimethylmetal precursors and NH3 or N2/H2 plasma. Preliminary depositions carried out using non-optimized process parameters resulted in reasonably uniform AlN and GaN films with wafer-level non-uniformities less than 1.5%. XPS survey scans detected 2.5-3.0 and 1.5-1.7 at.% O in these AlN and GaN thin films, respectively. C was detected only at the film surfaces and there were no C impurities in the bulk films as determined by XPS. Complementary SIMS analyses performed on the films deposited using NH3 plasma revealed the presence of O, C (both <1%) and H impurities in the films. GIXRD patterns exhibited polycrystalline AlN and GaN thin films with (hexagonal) wurtzite crystal structure. Crystallite sizes were 19.2 and 24.8 nm for AlN, and 10.2 and 9.3 nm for GaN films deposited using NH3 and N2/H2 plasma, respectively. The HR-TEM image of the GaN thin film deposited using NH3 plasma further revealed the existence of relatively large crystals in the film, which can extend along the film thickness.

value: A new ALD process for fabrication of conformal thin films of the amorphous solid electrolyte lithium borate-carbonate (LBCO) is presented. The degree of Li2CO3 incorporation can be tuned by adjusting deposition temperature, which enables control over ionic transport properties. The role of carbon in increasing conductivity has been elucidated both by first principles calculations and experiments. Increased Li2CO3 content increases the ionic mobility of the Li and O in the structure, increasing diffusion (and ionic conductivity). The films can be grown on high-aspect-ratio 3D structures with excellent uniformity, opening the door to 3D architectures for thin-film batteries.

value: The reaction mechanism and ligand stability of the Me3AuPMe3 - H2 plasma process in the steady growth regime has been investigated in a pump-type reactor. During the main reaction mechanism, the PMe 3 and CH 3 ligands of the precursor remain on the gold surface after chemisorption of the Me3AuPMe3 molecules, causing self-saturating behaviour during the precursor exposure. The ligands are removed by the H2 plasma exposure, resulting in the formation of CH4 and possibly (tri,di)methylphosphine/phosphine groups. A minor fraction of precursor decomposition occurs due to the desorption of the ligands from the surface, as this effect creates additional adsorption sites for the next precursor exposure in a decomposition experiment. For substrate temperatures above 100°C the amount of precursor decomposition increases with substrate temperature and at 120°C the decomposition becomes larger than the GPC of the ALD process. At all substrate temperatures the CH3 groups get removed from the surface over time, most likely in the form of CH4. This occurs faster at higher substrate temperatures. The desorption of the PMe3 groups from the surface, which increases with temperature, seems to be the main factor that determines the precursor decomposition behaviour. Importantly, precursor decomposition does not occur on a SiO2 surface, hence another reaction mechanism must be responsible for the nucleation of Au PE-ALD on this surface. Transmission IR measurements on SiO2 substrates indicate that Si-OH surface groups are consumed during the initial Me3AuPMe3 exposures, which makes them the most likely candidates to act as nucleation sites for the Me3AuPMe3 - H2 plasma process. Finally, using O2 plasma and H2O as co-reactants in a pump-type ALD system resulted in the formation of amorphous gold-containing phosphate films, whereas swapping the H2O exposure step with a H2 plasma resulted in the formation of metallic gold films.

Except for the only O2* process, processes which comprise a H2* step enable Pd growth at 100°C, displaying a clear difference in GPC ranked from high to low as follows: O2*+H2*>NH3*≈H2*>H2*+O2*. We report on the growth of indium nitride thin films using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) at low temperatures. The PECVD process was optimized to achieve high-quality InN films with a crystalline structure and a surface roughness of 0.73 nm. The films were grown on silicon substrates, and their properties were investigated by X-ray diffraction, Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The results show that the PECVD process is suitable for growing high-quality InN films at low temperatures.

value: The ALD behavior of Ru thin films was examined using Rudense and oxygen gas at growth temperature and pressure ranging from 250 to 270 C and 0.5 to 2.5 Torr, respectively. The heteroleptic configuration of the Rudense with EtCp and DMOPD ligands offered a suitable steric hindrance with high reactivity. The steady-state growth rate of the Ru films was 0.83 nm/cy on the Ta2O5, Si, and Ru substrates, which is almost tripled value compared to the ALD of the Ru film using similar Ru(DMPD)(EtCp) precursor. The films were well crystallized to metallic Ru phases with relatively random orientations. The resistivity of the thicker film > 20 nm was as low as 23 mu-ohm-cm and increased to 70 mu-ohm-cm at a thickness of 3.5 nm. The Ru film on Pt substrate exhibited a c-axis preferred growth behavior according to the (111)-preferred growth behavior of the Pt layer, resulting in a decreased growth rate (0.58 nm/cy). Smooth and uniform surface morphology of the Ru film was obtained at thicknesses below 5 nm, however, they became rough and showed many local protrusions on the Ta2O5 and Si substrates as the thickness of the Ru films increased. This was attributed to the excessively high reactivity between the Ru precursor and the active surface oxygen atoms on the already produced Ru nuclei as compared to the reaction between the precursor and substrate itself. Therefore, NH3 gas was pulsed after the O2 gas injection step to appropriately decrease the active surface oxygen density especially at the top part of the Ru nuclei, while the metallic properties of Ru films were unaffected. When the NH3 gas flow time was 1 s, the film morphology was greatly improved, whereas the excessive NH3 gas flow (30 s) induced significant degradation on the film morphology due to swelling of the Ru film on the Ta2O5 and Si substrates.

The reaction of trimethylaluminium (TMA) with alumina and the consecutive reaction of ammonia were studied using DRIFT, 1H MAS NMR, and elemental analysis. TMA reacted with dehydroxylated alumina in a saturating manner at temperatures from 353 to 573 K. Decomposition took place at 600 K and above. The methyl group density after the reaction was constant, 5-6 Me. A general reaction scheme for TMA reaction with oxide surfaces is proposed: TMA reacts with all the OH groups, forming methane and species (n = 2, 1 or 0). Simultaneously, reaction takes place with metal-oxygen bonds until a methyl group density of about 5 Me is achieved. Good conditions for AlN deposition by ALD from TMA and ammonia appear to be any temperature below 573 K for the TMA reaction and temperatures in excess of 623 K, preferably 823 K, for the ammonia reaction.

This paper presents the HCPA-ALD (Hydrothermal Chemical Vapor Deposition) growth of crystalline AlN, GaN, and AlxGa1-xNx thin films at low temperatures using trimethylmetal precursors and NH3 or N2/H2 plasma. Preliminary depositions carried out using non-optimized process parameters resulted in reasonably uniform AlN and GaN films with wafer-level non-uniformities less than 1.5%. XPS survey scans detected 2.5-3.0 and 1.5-1.7 at.% O in these AlN and GaN thin films, respectively. C was detected only at the film surfaces and there were no C impurities in the bulk films as determined by XPS. Complementary SIMS analyses performed on the films deposited using NH3 plasma revealed the presence of O, C (both <1%) and H impurities in the films. GIXRD patterns exhibited polycrystalline AlN and GaN thin films with (hexagonal) wurtzite crystal structure. Crystallite sizes were 19.2 and 24.8 nm for AlN, and 10.2 and 9.3 nm for GaN films deposited using NH3 and N2/H2 plasma, respectively. The HR-TEM image of the GaN thin film deposited using NH3 plasma further revealed the existence of relatively large crystals in the film, which can extend along the film thickness.

To overcome these problems we designed an ALD lanthanum precursor: tris( N,N8-diisopropylacetamidinato!lanthanum, La(iPrAMD)3 . The synthesis and properties of this compound have been described, 10 and it is now commercially available.11 It is the most volatile lanthanum compound known, subliming at 80 °C at a pressure of 0.04 Torr.

Furthermore, it reacts rapidly with water, so it can be used for CVD and ALD of La2O3 . A problem of using water for ALD of lanthanum oxide is that the film reacts with water vapor to form lanthanum hydroxide.

Lanthanum hydroxide then desorbs water continuously even after a long purge time and reacts with the next pulse of lanthanum precursor by a CVD reaction, ruining the self-limited nature of the ALD reaction. To overcome this water adsorption/desorption problem we deposited alternating layers ( ,a few nm thick ! of La2O3 and Al2O3 to form a nanolaminate film. The aluminum oxide layers are impervious to water, limiting the water diffusion to only the thin La2O3 layer closest to the surface.

Therefore the excess water in this thin La2O3 layer can be desorbed without using an excessively long purge time.

Thin films of MoO3 deposited on Si(111) and Al2O3 substrates by atomic layer deposition have been investigated by x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and Raman spectroscopy for detailed characterization of composition and morphology.

Comparison of angle resolved x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (ARXPS) and XPS depth profiles based on Ar sputtering is reported. Sputtering induces a reduction of molybdenum in MoO3 from IV to metallic Mo as the interface toward Si is approached, whereas ARXPS on a 10 nm thin film shows that Mo(VI) remains outside the interface toward Si where lower valent molybdenum compounds are formed.

The crystallization behavior of the 40 nm amorphous films of MoO3 on Al2O3 was studied ex situ for samples subjected to annealing in air (8 min at 400 /C14 C, 4, 6, and 7.5 min at 600 /C14 C). These treatments resulted in conversion of amorphous MoO3 via b-MoO3 to orthorhombic a-MoO3 as evidenced by XRD, AFM and Raman spectroscopy.

The x-ray data show that the film annealed for 8 min at 400 /C14 C consists of crystalline b-MoO3 with small impurities of a-MoO3. However, when annealed at 600 /C14 C for 4 and 7.5 min, the films consist of polycrystalline a-MoO3 and fully crystallized orthorhombic a-MoO3, respectively.

The conversion of b- to a-MoO3 is reconstructive. For bulk samples the conversion is reported to take place between 250 and 450 /C14 C, in good agreement with present observations.
